lines.text: Two attacks. One day.
On October 28th, the hostel internet died twice. Both times, we caught exactly why.
Every device on the hostel network first asks one question: who is the router?
The real router, a MikroTik, answers with its address. All internet traffic then flows through it.
lines.say: The real router, a Micro-Tik, answers with its address. All internet traffic then flows through it.

lines.text: 5:34 and 3 seconds. Another device starts answering instead. Its message: I am the router.
The laptop believed it. So did two other devices nearby.
From that moment, every packet went to the impostor. 71 packets out. Zero came back.
That's why Discord shows five thousand milliseconds, friends can't hear you, and pages load forever, with no error.
Nothing comes back, so nothing can even fail properly.
Two and a half minutes, until the cable was pulled. netbug recorded every second.
lines.say: Two and a half minutes, until the cable was pulled. Net-bug recorded every second.

lines.text: To be sure, we removed the protection. And waited.
At 3:28 that afternoon, it happened again.
Same device.
Same address.
Same lie.
42 packets out. Zero back.
Four more devices lost the router, and the capture caught the attacker looking up its next victim: one it had already cut off that morning.
Every detail matched. Not a broken router. Not a bad cable.
Someone on this network is cutting people off. On purpose.
The fix on this laptop: pin the real router's address. Fake replies are simply ignored.
Reconnecting then worked instantly. But the pin protects only this laptop, and only its outgoing traffic.
For the hostel team: find this device on the MikroTik, then turn on client isolation and ARP protection. That protects everyone.
lines.say: For the hostel team: find this device on the Micro-Tik, then turn on client isolation and A.R.P. protection. That protects everyone.
